newsitem.title: INDIA: ADB wants India to divest in oil sector.
newsitem.headline: ADB wants India to divest in oil sector.

text.p: India must speed up the pace of divestment in its state-run oil companies or face the prospect of losing badly-needed aid funding, an Asian Development Bank (ADB) official told Reuters on Wednesday.

"We will have to wait about a year and, if they don't do it, we will have to stop the second tranche of loans," C.S Chung, a senior ADB project officer, said on the margins of an international oil and gas conference in the Indian capital.

Chung was referring to projects, partly-funded by the ADB, with India's state-run Oil and Natural Gas Corp (ONGC), and the Gas Authority of India Ltd (GAIL), to promote accelerated exploration of domestic oil and gas resources, and speed the movement away from an administered-price regime.

India's appetite for petroleum products is growing at the rate of eight percent annually, experts at the conference estimated. Its natural gas demand is expected to rise to about 150 million cubic metres a day by the year 2000.
Today, India produces 63 million cubic metres a day against a demand for 89 million cubic metres a day.

The ADB has disbursed one tranche of a $250 million loan to India's petroleum and natural gas ministry, Chung said, but the second tranche might be cancelled or delayed if the government did not reduce its holdings in ONGC and GAIL.
Chung said the ADB wanted the Indian government to divest up to 20 percent of its holding in ONGC, and 30 percent in GAIL. India has only divested a "few percent" so far in either company, he said.
"We know that the market situation is not so favourable now in India or abroad for such a divestment," Chung said.
"And government is now trying to restructure ONGC's organisation and management. We don't want to wait, but we'll have to wait."

Chung said the ADB had funded four major projects in India over the last five years, totalling $1 billion. It had provided $2.5 million worth of technical assistance for several other projects, he added.
Many other projects, aimed at boosting the use of liquefied natural gas (LNG) in India, are now being considered by the bank for aid, Chung said.

A project to construct a 1,700-km-long pipeline carrying LNG from the Gandhar fields of the ONGC through the western states of Gujarat, Rajasthan and Haryana at a cost of about $530 million has almost completed the approval process, Chung said.
"This is a firm ADB project for 1997, and it will be approved in the second half of this year," Chung told delegates to the conference.
"ADB and co-funders will give a loan of $235 million. The rest, about $295 million, is to be raised by GAIL and through commercial borrowings."
Once in place, the pipeline will help minimise transportation costs, improve reliability of delivery, boost safety and environmental compliance, Chung added.
India has sought assistance from the ADB to build a $650-million LNG terminal project in the southern states of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, Chung said.

It envisages the construction of a terminal at Ennore port near Madras city in Tamil Nadu state, and another at Mangalore port in Karantaka state, Chung said, as well as facilities for the import, storage and regasification of LNG.
Also on the drawing board is a $700 million project to build a gas pipeline to supply India's southern states, Chung added.
"GAIL would like to supply natural gas southwards," Chung said. "So far it has been restricted to northern regions where the reserves are." Chung gave no additional details of projects.
